head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Remembers the answer for every pair of substrings already examined
Recursion revisits the same subproblems many times
Identical strings are trivially scrambles of each other
Cheapest base case, ends the recursion early
Different letter multisets can never be scrambles
Cut at `i` and keep the two halves in the same order
The "no swap" case of a split
`go(a[:i], b[n - i:]) and go(a[i:], b[:n - i])`
Cut at `i` and swap: the front of `a` must match the back of `b`

p: `s1 = "great"`, `s2 = "rgeat"`, `n = 5`. The first cut that works is `i = 2`.

head: Call
Check
Result
rows: Not equal, same letters, try cuts
`go("g","r")` is False (letters differ); swapped `go("g","t")` is False

p: Scrambling may swap the two parts, so after cutting `a` at `i`, either its front part lines up with the front of `b` (no swap) or with the last `i` characters of `b` (swap). Trying both for every `i` covers every way the first split can happen.

bullets: Time: O(n^4) in the worst case. There are O(n^2) distinct pairs of equal-length substrings that appear (start of `a` and start of `b` for each length), and each does O(n) cut work plus O(n log n) sorting.
Space: O(n^3) for the memo table and the substrings it stores.

87.takeaway: Recursively try every cut with and without a swap, prune with an equal-letters check, and memoize so repeated substring pairs are solved once.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A fake head in front of the sorted list
Inserting at the very front should not need a special case
`cur` is the node being inserted; `nxt` remembers the rest of the input before the links change
You are about to re-link a node
`prev = dummy` then `while prev.next and prev.next.val < cur.val`
Walk the sorted list until the next node is not smaller than `cur`
Splice `cur` in between `prev` and its old next
Move to the next unsorted node

p: `head = [4,2,1,3]`. The list hanging off `dummy` is the sorted part.
Inserting `cur` overwrites `cur.next`, which pointed to the unsorted remainder. Without `nxt` the rest of the input would be lost.

bullets: Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, because each insertion may walk across the whole sorted part. Already-sorted input is also O(n^2) here since the scan starts from the front each time.
Space: O(1) extra, nodes are re-linked in place.

147.takeaway: Insertion sort on a linked list: detach each node, scan the sorted list from a dummy head to find its place, and splice it in.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Pairs up the characters at the same position
Comparing two strings position by position
`sum(a == b for a, b in zip(...))`
Counts positions where the digits match: the bulls
Multiset intersection: for each digit the smaller of the two counts
How many digits the two strings share, with multiplicity
Total number of shared digits, bulls and cows together
The shared digits that are not in the right place: the cows
Splitting one total into two parts

p: Shared total is 4. Only position 1 matches (`8` and `8`), so bulls = 1, cows = 4 − 1 = 3, giving `"1A3B"`.

blocks.h: Why does subtracting bulls give the cows?
p: Every bull is also a shared digit, so it is inside the intersection total. The remaining shared digits are in the secret and in the guess but not at the same position, which is the definition of a cow. Taking the minimum of the counts also makes sure each secret digit is used at most once.

bullets: Time: O(n) for the pass and the counters.
Space: O(1), at most 10 distinct digits.

299.takeaway: Bulls are position matches; total shared digits come from a Counter intersection; cows are total minus bulls.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Fixes the top and bottom rows of the rectangle
Reducing a 2D problem to a 1D one
`cols[j]` is the column-j sum between `top` and `bottom`
Compressing several rows into one row
Running prefix sum of `cols` from the left
Subarray sum = difference of two prefix sums
All earlier prefix sums, always in order
You need the smallest earlier value that is at least some bound
Index of the first prefix `>= run - k`
Finding the smallest valid candidate in a sorted list
The sum `run - prefix` is `<= k` and as large as possible for this right edge
Insert the current prefix, keeping the list sorted

p: Other row pairs give at most 2 as well, so the answer is `2`.

blocks.h: Why the smallest prefix that is `>= run - k`?
p: For a fixed right end, the sum is `run - prefix`. We need `run - prefix <= k`, which means `prefix >= run - k`. Among the allowed prefixes, the smallest one makes `run - prefix` the largest, so it is the best candidate. A binary search on the sorted list finds it.

bullets: Time: O(m^2 · n log n). The row pair loops cost m^2, and each scan over columns does a binary search (plus an insertion that shifts list items). Choose the smaller dimension as the row side when one is much bigger.
Space: O(n) for `cols` and `prefixes`.

363.takeaway: Fix two rows, collapse to a 1D array, and use a sorted list of prefix sums plus binary search to find the best subarray sum not above k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `for h in range(12) for m in range(60)`
Every valid time on the watch: hours 0 to 11, minutes 0 to 59
The search space is small enough to enumerate
Number of 1 bits in `h`, i.e. LEDs lit for the hour
Keep only times whose total lit LEDs match
Format hour without padding and minute with two digits

p: `turnedOn = 1`. Only times where exactly one bit is set across hour and minute qualify.

blocks.h: Why enumerate times instead of choosing LEDs?
p: There are only 12 × 60 = 720 candidate times. Looping over them and counting bits is simpler than choosing which LEDs to light, and it automatically skips impossible times such as hour 13 or minute 61.

bullets: Time: O(720), a constant.
Space: O(1) besides the output list.

401.takeaway: Try all 720 valid times and keep those whose hour bits plus minute bits equal the number of lit LEDs.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `starts = sorted((s, i) for i, (s, _) in enumerate(intervals))`
List of (start, original index) pairs in start order
You need to search by start but report the original index
Only the sorted starts, for binary search
`bisect` works on a plain list of numbers
Index of the first start `>= e`
Smallest value that is at least a bound
The original index at that position, or `-1` if no start is large enough

blocks.h: Why is the first start `>= end` the right one?
p: The right interval needs start at least `end` and, among those, the smallest start. In a sorted list that is exactly the first element at or after `end`, which is what `bisect_left` returns. Because every start is unique there are no ties to break.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting plus one binary search per interval.
Space: O(n).

436.takeaway: Sort the starts once and answer each interval with a binary search for the first start at or after its end.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: The loop below would produce an empty string for 0
Handle the sign separately and work with a positive number
Converting negatives is easier on magnitudes
Quotient and remainder in one step; `r` is the next digit from the right
Peeling off digits in some base
Collect digits in the order produced (lowest first)
Put the digits in most-significant-first order

p: Digits collected `2, 0, 2`, reversed they read `"202"`. Check: 2·49 + 0·7 + 2 = 100.
The remainder gives the least significant digit first, but a number is written starting from the most significant one. Appending is cheap, so we collect first and reverse once.

bullets: Time: O(log_7 |num|), one step per digit.
Space: O(log_7 |num|) for the digits.

504.takeaway: Repeatedly take `num % 7` as the next digit and `num // 7` as the rest, then reverse the digits and reattach the sign.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Number of valid records so far with `a` absences (0 or 1) and a current streak of `l` late days at the end (0 to 2)
The future depends only on a few summary numbers
The empty record: no absence, no late streak
Add a present day `P`: streak resets to 0
Transition that keeps the absence count
Add an absent day `A`, allowed only if none so far; streak resets
A limit of fewer than 2 absences
Add a late day `L`; a third in a row is forbidden
Keep numbers small, as the problem asks

p: `n = 2`. After one day: `(0,0)`: 1 (P), `(1,0)`: 1 (A), `(0,1)`: 1 (L). After the second day:
Total = 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8. (There are 9 records of length 2; only `AA` is excluded.)

head: State
Count
Where it comes from
rows: A from (0,0), P from (1,0), A from (0,1)

p: To know whether adding a character keeps the record eligible we only need how many `A` have appeared (0 or 1) and how many `L` end the record (0, 1 or 2). Everything else about the past is irrelevant, so 2 × 3 states are enough.

bullets: Time: O(n) with a constant 6 states and 3 transitions each.
Space: O(1).

552.takeaway: Count records with a small DP (dynamic programming) over (absences so far, trailing lates) and add them up after n days.

blocks.h: Why the check at the top of the loop?
p: The first condition runs before each token. If the stack is empty but we are past index 0, the outer tag has already been closed, so extra text or a second top-level tag makes the whole snippet invalid. It also forces index 0 to start with a tag, because plain text with an empty stack is rejected.

bullets: Time: O(n), every character is visited a constant number of times (the CDATA search jumps forward).
Space: O(n) for the stack in the worst case.

591.takeaway: Scan left to right with a stack of open tag names, skipping CDATA literally and rejecting any text outside the single outer tag.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Smallest and largest value seen so far (arrays are sorted, so ends are the extremes)
Pair the new array's largest with the smallest seen earlier
One of the two best combinations
Pair the new array's smallest with the largest seen earlier
Update after using the old values, so a pair never uses one array twice

p: The answer is `4`.

blocks.h: Why only the first and last elements?
p: The farthest apart two numbers from different arrays can be is between a minimum of one and a maximum of the other, and in a sorted array those are the ends. Updating `lo` and `hi` after computing the candidates guarantees both numbers come from different arrays.

bullets: Time: O(m), one step per array.
Space: O(1).

624.takeaway: Walk the arrays once, pairing each array's ends with the smallest and largest value seen in earlier arrays.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Nodes in decreasing order of value, the current "right spine" of the tree
New node for the next number
Building the tree as numbers arrive
`while stack and stack[-1].val < x: last = stack.pop()`
Pop all smaller nodes; the last popped one is the biggest of them
Smaller elements to the left become the left subtree
The popped chain becomes this node's left child
The node hangs on the right of the next larger one
The bottom of the stack is the maximum, the root

p: The root is 6 with left child 3 (whose right chain is 2 then 1) and right child 5 (left child 0).

The maximum binary tree puts every number's nearest larger neighbours above it. A new value `x` pops everything smaller, and those nodes lie to its left in the array, so they form its left subtree. If a larger node remains on the stack, `x` is the newest element to its right, so `x` becomes its right child (replacing a previous right child, which was already moved under `x`).

bullets: Time: O(n), each node is pushed and popped once.
Space: O(n) for the stack.

654.takeaway: A decreasing stack builds the tree in one pass: pop smaller nodes to be the new node's left child, then hang it on the larger node that remains.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: You need the size to plan the split
Every part gets `size` nodes and the first `extra` parts get one more
Splitting as evenly as possible with earlier parts larger
The head of this part is the current node
`for _ in range(size + (1 if i < extra else 0) - 1)`
Walk to the last node of this part (length minus one steps)
Reaching the end of a segment
Cut the link after this part and step to the start of the next one, in one assignment
Detaching a segment without losing the rest

p: On the right side Python first evaluates `(None, node.next)`, so the old next node is remembered. Then it sets `node.next = None` (the cut) and `node` to the remembered next node. Doing the two steps in separate lines would need a temporary variable.

bullets: Time: O(n + k), one pass to count and one pass to cut.
Space: O(1) besides the output list of k heads.

725.takeaway: Count the nodes, give each part `n // k` nodes (the first `n % k` parts one extra), and cut the list at those boundaries.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of `X` and `O` on the board
Move order can be checked by counts
True if player `p` fills any row, column or diagonal
`X` moves first, so `x` is either equal to `o` or one more
If `X` has won, `X` made the last move, so `x` must be one more than `o`
The game stops at the first win
If `O` has won, `O` moved last, so counts must be equal

p: All checks pass, so the result is `True`. For `["XXX","   ","OOO"]` both players have a line, and `wins('X')` demands `x == o + 1` but `x == o == 3`, so it is `False`.

blocks.h: Why is checking counts plus winners enough?
p: A reachable board must have a legal move count and must not continue after someone has won. Counts handle the order of play, and the winner conditions handle the stopping rule. If both players had won, the two conditions contradict each other (one needs `x == o + 1`, the other `x == o`), so it is rejected automatically.

bullets: Time: O(1), the board has 9 cells.
Space: O(1).

794.takeaway: Check that X leads by 0 or 1 move, and that a winner is consistent with who moved last.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Reads the row from right to left: the horizontal flip
Turns 0 into 1 and 1 into 0: the inversion

blocks.h: Why can both steps be one pass?
p: Flipping moves elements and inverting changes each value; neither depends on neighbours, so doing both while reading the row from the back gives the same result as two separate passes.

bullets: Time: O(n^2), each cell is read once.
Space: O(n^2) for the new matrix.

832.takeaway: Read each row backwards and replace every value `v` by `1 - v`.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Coordinates of the `1` cells in each image
Only the ones matter for an overlap
The shift that would move a `1` of `img1` onto a `1` of `img2`
Each pair of ones votes for one shift
Counts how many pairs vote for each shift
The most popular shift is the best overlap; `default=0` handles an image with no ones

p: The best shift gets 3 votes, so the answer is `3`.

A shift lines up a given pair of ones exactly when it equals their coordinate difference. Every shift's overlap is therefore the number of pairs that produce that difference, so the shift with the most votes gives the largest overlap. Cells moved off the grid are never counted because only real ones are compared.

bullets: Time: O(A · B), where A and B are the numbers of ones (at most n^2 each, so O(n^4)).
Space: O(number of distinct shifts), up to O(n^2).

835.takeaway: Let every pair of ones vote for the shift that lines them up, and the most-voted shift is the maximum overlap.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Index of the bit currently being looked at, counting from the right
Position of the previous 1 bit, `None` before the first one
Gap between this 1 and the previous 1

p: The first 1 bit has no earlier 1 to measure against, so it only records its position. Without this check the first gap would be measured from a made-up position.

bullets: Time: O(log n), one step per bit.
Space: O(1).

868.takeaway: Scan the bits from the right, remember where the previous 1 was, and keep the largest distance between consecutive 1s.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: With only the first letter movable, the only operation is a rotation
The move set decides the strategy
The string rotated left by `i` positions
For `k >= 2` any arrangement is reachable, so the sorted string is the best
The goal is the smallest possible string

p: `s = "cba"`, `k = 1`: all rotations.
The smallest is `"acb"`. With `s = "baaca"`, `k = 3` the result is the sorted string `"aaabc"`.

blocks.h: Why is any order possible when `k >= 2`?
p: With two movable letters you can effectively swap neighbouring letters (moving the second letter to the end, then rotating the rest around), and repeated adjacent swaps can build any ordering. So the best result is simply all letters in sorted order.

bullets: Time: O(n^2) for `k == 1` (n rotations of length n, compared character by character) and O(n log n) otherwise.
Space: O(n) for the strings built.

899.takeaway: One movable letter only rotates the string, so try all rotations; two or more can reach every ordering, so just sort.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Union of counters: for each letter keep the larger count
Subtraction keeping only positive leftovers: what `need` asks for that `w` lacks
Checking if a word covers a requirement
An empty counter is falsy, so `not` means the word covers everything

p: `words2 = ["e","o"]` gives `need = {e:1, o:1}`.

blocks.h: Why merge all words of `words2` into one requirement?
p: A word is universal when it covers every word of `words2`. For each letter the word must have at least the largest count that any single word of `words2` asks for. So one combined "max count per letter" requirement is equivalent to checking each word separately, and it needs only one comparison per candidate.

bullets: Time: O(total length of words1 + words2).
Space: O(1), counters have at most 26 keys.

916.takeaway: Combine words2 into one per-letter maximum requirement, then keep the words of words1 that meet it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of distinct subsequences that end with the letter `c`
Counting by last character avoids double counting
The single letter `c`, plus every existing subsequence with `c` appended
The new value replaces the old one, because it already includes everything the old one counted
Duplicate letters would otherwise be counted twice

p: `s = "abc"`.
For `"aba"` the last `a` sets `end[a] = 1 + 3 = 4` (replacing 1), and the total is 4 + 2 = 6.

Appending `a` to every earlier subsequence, including those that already ended with `a`, creates every distinct subsequence ending in `a` that can be formed so far. The old ones ending in `a` are a subset of these, so keeping both would count the same strings twice.

bullets: Time: O(26 · n), the sum covers at most 26 letters per character.
Space: O(26).

940.takeaway: Track how many distinct subsequences end with each letter; each new character recomputes its own count from the total so far.

Simulating the reveal process on positions instead of values
Cards in the order they must be revealed
The next revealed position receives the next smallest card
The next position goes to the bottom of the deck
The "move the top card to the bottom" rule
Skip the move after the last card

p: The reveal process is fixed by the number of cards, not by their values. Running it on indices tells us which position is revealed first, second and so on, so we just place the smallest card at the first, the next smallest at the second, etc.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting, O(n) for the simulation.
Space: O(n).

950.takeaway: Simulate the reveal on positions with a queue, and give the sorted cards to those positions in the order they are revealed.

Meaning

rows: Fast check for an exact match, case included
Maps the lowercase word to the first list word that has that lowercase form
Lowercases the word and replaces every vowel with `*`
A key where all vowel variants look the same
Maps each vowel-masked key to its first word
Try exact, then case-insensitive, then vowel-masked, then empty string

p: `wordlist = ["KiTe","kite","hare","Hare"]`.
`setdefault` stores a value only if the key is new, so later words never overwrite earlier ones. That implements the rule that the first matching word in the list is the one returned.

Space: O(total characters) for the three lookup structures.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Greedy on the biggest candidates first
Triangle inequality for the sides `nums[i]` (longest) and the next two
The first valid triple from the top has the biggest perimeter
No triple of consecutive sides works

p: `nums = [2,1,2]` sorted descending: `[2,2,1]`.

For a given longest side, the best partners are the two next-largest values, because they make the sum of the two shorter sides as large as possible. If even those do not beat the longest side, no other pair will, so that side can be dropped and the search moves on. The first success is the largest possible perimeter.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

976.takeaway: Sort descending and take the first three consecutive lengths that satisfy the triangle inequality.
